newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: INTERVIEW - Guatemala's Guatel readies for selloff.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Guatemala's Guatel readies for selloff.

text.p: Guatemala's state phone company Guatel has taken on hundreds of millions of dollars in loans for improvements with an eye toward impressing potential foreign buyers later this year, a Guatel executive said.
The projects include a national fiber optic ring, administration software, new public pay phones, 100,000 new lines by July 15 and more digitalized lines.

"All of these projects increase the value of the company. Our goal is that the buyer find Guatel is not stagnant, even though it's being sold," Giovanni Musella, deputy chief of operations of the Guatemalan Telecommunications Company (Guatel), told Reuters in a recent interview.

Guatel executives are in New York this week choosing an investment bank to manage the sale of the phone company. The four banks that have submitted proposals are C.S. First Boston, Lehman Brothers, Salomon Brothers and J.P. Morgan.

Guatel's new owner, to be chosen by July 15 after an international bidding process, will take on the loan commitments the government leaves behind. But the new lines and other projects will pay for themselves, Musella said.
The buyer of Guatel will have to make further investments to bring the inadequate phone system up to standard.

"I calculate that the investor will have to put in some $300 million to make Guatel competitive at a worldwide level and to maintain it in a dominant position within the Guatemalam market," Musella said.

Guatemala currently has 326,000 working lines -- about three telephones for every 100 people -- and a million requests backlogged. At 20 workers per 1000 lines, Guatel is far more inefficient than the international standard of four.
Despite its inefficiency, the phone company is one of the government's biggest cash cows.

Musella said Guatel's net profit in 1996 was approximately $100 million, with 45 percent going to the government, 40 percent reinvested in Guatel, and the rest divided among employee profit sharing, an emergency fund and pension funds.
Musella would not disclose the estimated worth of Guatel. "The price will be based on the market opportunity," he said.

The market will be completely open under a new telecommunications law. Other companies will be able to construct infrastructure to connect to Guatel, or rent Guatel lines for international and national services.
To make Guatel more competitive when other phone companies enter the market, the company effected Feb. 15 a drastic decrease in rates for international calls.
The company that buys Guatel will take on all current obligations to phone company employees, including severance pay and pensions.
Guatel workers will also get five percent of the shares in the new company which is free to retain or sell the other 95 percent wherever it wants.
Musella minimized the possibility of delays in Congress or the courts.
The Constitutional Court is studying a legal challenge to the new telecommunications law, but the court has not suspended the law while it considers the challenge.
Congress is scheduled to pass in March another law legalizing privatizations. Since the ruling party also enjoys a majority in the legislature, Musella doesn't anticipate significant opposition.
"Everything that could possibly tie up the process ... we've got a legal team ready to solve it," Musella said.
